title: Converting a one-car garage into a small machine shop: power, layout, budget
summary: Floorplan-first: where the lathe, mill, welder, and circuits sit in a ~12×20 one-car bay, then the power and budget that make that map real.

blocks.eyebrow: Floorplan first — machines and circuits on the map
blocks.title: Draw the shop before you buy the subpanel
blocks.body: A one-car garage (~12×20 ft usable) only works as a small machine shop if heavy machines, chip paths, and receptacles share one plan. This page starts with where things sit. Power sizing and budget follow the drawing.

items.label: Example subpanel for light metal work

nodes.title: North wall — lathe
nodes.detail: Long axis parallel to the wall. Tailstock toward the service door so stock can stick out without blocking egress. Leave ~36 in clear in front of the apron.

nodes.title: Northeast corner — mill / drill
nodes.detail: Beside the lathe so you can walk a part between spindles without crossing the welder arc zone. Keep the quill clear of the overhead door track.

nodes.title: South wall — weld / grind cell
nodes.detail: Against a masonry or protected wall with ventilation path to the outdoors. Keep grind sparks away from solvent and paper storage.

nodes.title: West wall — bench + vise
nodes.detail: Under the best daylight or LED run. Hand tools hang above; low cabinets below. Aisle down the center stays open for a cart.

nodes.title: Southeast — compressor + vac
nodes.detail: Near the overhead door for exhaust and hose reach. Noise and vibration stay off the precision machine pads.

nodes.title: Center aisle
nodes.detail: Keep a continuous walk path ~36 in wide from the man-door to the overhead door. No permanent machine in the middle.

blocks.heading: Circuit map — receptacles follow the machines

nodes.title: Subpanel on the east wall
nodes.detail: Near the service entrance. Labeled breakers. Lockable cover. This is the shop's power hub — not a tangle of extension cords.

nodes.title: 240 V / 20–30 A at lathe and welder
nodes.detail: Hard-located receptacles or whip drops at the machine pads. Do not share a single 240 V run between weld and spindle if both can run together.

nodes.title: 120 V duplex every 6–8 ft on bench walls
nodes.detail: Dedicated circuits for compressor and dust collector. GFCI where code and damp walls demand it.

nodes.title: Lighting on its own circuit
nodes.detail: Two LED shop-light runs (north and south) so a tool breaker trip does not leave you in the dark mid-cut.

nodes.title: Emergency stop / disconnects
nodes.detail: Within reach of each powered machine. Welder and compressor get local disconnects you can see from the work zone.

blocks.heading: Layout rules that keep the map honest

items.label: Place heaviest machines first
items.detail: Lathe and mill pads lock the rest of the drawing.

items.label: Chip and spark zones do not overlap paper or solvent
items.detail: Weld-grind cell stays south; precision spindles stay north.

items.label: Every powered pad has a visible disconnect path
items.detail: No machine that can only be killed from the house panel.

items.label: Aisle stays clear after the first real job
items.detail: If the first project blocks the man-door, the floorplan failed — redraw before buying more tools.

blocks.heading: Build order that respects the floorplan
items: Tape the machine footprints and aisle on the empty floor. Walk it with a cart. Adjust before any concrete anchors.
Mark receptacle and lighting drops on the same tape plan. Photograph the marked floor.
Install the subpanel and the circuits that land on those marks.
Roll machines onto their pads, level, and wire. Prove one end-to-end job before expanding the map.

blocks.title: Power work is not a floorplan sketch
blocks.body: This page is a spatial planning artifact with example loads. Feeder sizing, grounding, and permitting belong to local code and a qualified electrician — especially anything 240 V or a new subpanel.

blocks.heading: Sanity check
blocks.prompt: On this floorplan-first approach, what should you place before ordering the subpanel?
options: The full tooling catalog for five years out
Taped machine footprints, aisle, and receptacle marks on the floor
A second welder for overflow work
blocks.explanation: The circuit map and subpanel size follow where machines and aisles actually sit. Tape the bay first so power lands on real pads.

blocks.heading: Next move
blocks.body: Tonight: tape the lathe, mill, weld cell, and aisle. Tomorrow: mark the receptacles on that same plan. Power and budget only after the map stops changing.
